events.title: The world of 1 January 1920
events.text: The First World War ended just over a year ago and has redrawn the map. The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires have collapsed, new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes are emerging, and Britain and France rule the largest empires in history. Aviation is young: the first powered flight was only 17 years ago, and thousands of surplus war aircraft and pilots are about to create the first commercial airlines.

events.title: Syria and Lebanon fall under French mandate
events.text: French troops defeat Faisal's Arab army at the Battle of Maysalun on 24 July 1920 and enter Damascus, ending the short-lived Arab Kingdom of Syria. The San Remo conference in April had already given France the mandates over Syria and Lebanon and Britain those over Iraq and Palestine. France divides its mandate into smaller states, including an enlarged Lebanon proclaimed on 1 September 1920.

events.title: Egypt becomes independent
events.text: Britain declares Egypt independent on 28 February 1922, ending the protectorate it had imposed in 1914. Egypt becomes a kingdom, but Britain keeps control of defence, the Suez Canal and Sudan, so independence is only partial. British troops did not leave the canal zone until 1956.

events.title: The Irish Free State is born
events.text: After the Irish War of Independence (1919-21) and the Anglo-Irish Treaty, the Irish Free State is established on 6 December 1922 as a self-governing dominion. Six counties in the north opt out and stay in the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland, creating the border that still exists today. A civil war between supporters and opponents of the treaty was fought in 1922-23.

events.title: The Soviet Union is founded
events.text: On 30 December 1922 the Russian, Ukrainian, Byelorussian and Transcaucasian Soviet republics sign the treaty creating the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia had been brought under Soviet control between 1920 and 1921 and are joined as one federation. Central Asia is reorganised into new republics in the following years, and by 1956 the union has fifteen republics.

events.title: The Republic of Turkey
events.text: After Mustafa Kemal's forces win the Turkish War of Independence, the Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923 replaces the Treaty of Sevres and fixes Turkey's modern borders. The Republic of Turkey is proclaimed on 29 October 1923 with Kemal as its first president; the sultanate had been abolished in 1922 and the caliphate followed in 1924. A population exchange moved well over a million Orthodox Christians and Muslims between Greece and Turkey.

events.title: The Mongolian People's Republic
events.text: Outer Mongolia declared autonomy from China in 1911 and was occupied by Chinese forces in 1919. After a Soviet-backed revolution in 1921, the Mongolian People's Republic is proclaimed on 26 November 1924, the world's second socialist state after Soviet Russia. The Republic of China only formally recognised Mongolian independence in 1946.

events.title: Japan creates Manchukuo
events.text: After the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, Japan's Kwantung Army occupies Manchuria and proclaims the state of Manchukuo on 1 March 1932, with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as its figurehead. The League of Nations' Lytton Commission rejected Japan's claim, and Japan left the League in 1933. Manchukuo remained under Japanese control until 1945.

events.title: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
events.text: Abdulaziz Ibn Saud captured Ha'il in 1921 and the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina, in 1925. On 23 September 1932 he unites his realms as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Oil, discovered in the Eastern Province in 1938, would transform the country's future.

events.title: Iraq becomes independent
events.text: Iraq, created from three Ottoman provinces and ruled by Britain under a League of Nations mandate, becomes independent on 3 October 1932 and joins the League as a sovereign state. Britain keeps air bases and strong influence under a treaty signed in 1930.

events.title: Persia becomes Iran
events.text: On 21 March 1935 Reza Shah asks foreign governments to call his country Iran, the name its people had long used for it, instead of Persia. The change reflected a drive to modernise the state and stress its Aryan and ancient roots.

events.title: Italy annexes Ethiopia
events.text: Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935, and its troops enter Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936. On 9 May Mussolini proclaims the annexation, and Ethiopia, Eritrea and Italian Somaliland are joined as Italian East Africa. The League of Nations' sanctions were weak, a failure that badly damaged its credibility. Emperor Haile Selassie's speech to the League in June 1936 became one of the most famous of the era.

events.title: The Anschluss: Germany annexes Austria
events.text: On 12 March 1938 German troops cross into Austria, and on 13 March the country is declared part of the German Reich. A plebiscite in April reported overwhelming approval but was held under Nazi control. The union violated the peace treaties of 1919, and Britain and France did not intervene.

events.title: Munich Agreement: the Sudetenland goes to Germany
events.text: At the Munich Conference of 29-30 September 1938, Britain, France, Italy and Germany agree that Czechoslovakia must hand its border region, the Sudetenland, to Germany. About three million ethnic Germans lived there, and Czechoslovakia was not invited to the talks. German troops occupy the region from 1 October, while Poland and Hungary also take small border areas.

events.title: Czechoslovakia is dismantled
events.text: On 14 March 1939 Slovakia declares independence under German protection, and on 15 March German troops occupy the Czech lands, which become the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. Hungary annexes Carpatho-Ukraine. Britain and France had promised at Munich to guarantee the rest of Czechoslovakia but did nothing, and many historians see the occupation as the end of appeasement.

events.title: Italy invades Albania
events.text: Italy invades Albania on 7 April 1939 and King Zog flees the country; the Albanian crown is then offered to Italy's king, Victor Emmanuel III. The invasion gave Mussolini a base on the Balkan peninsula, which he used to attack Greece in October 1940.

events.title: Turkey annexes Hatay
events.text: The Sanjak of Alexandretta, a territory of the French mandate of Syria with both Turkish and Arab inhabitants, votes to join Turkey in 1939 and is annexed on 23 June as Hatay Province. Syria never fully accepted the loss, and France agreed partly to win Turkey's friendship as war with Germany approached.

events.title: Siam becomes Thailand
events.text: Siam, which had avoided colonisation by balancing between Britain and France, is officially renamed Thailand on 24 June 1939 under Prime Minister Phibun, meaning the land of the free. The name was changed back to Siam briefly after the war and then settled as Thailand in 1949.

events.title: Poland is partitioned
events.text: Germany invades Poland on 1 September 1939, starting the Second World War, and the Soviet Union attacks from the east on 17 September. On 28 September the two powers agree a new border, following the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact signed on 23 August. Germany annexes western Poland and occupies the rest, while the USSR takes the eastern regions, home to many Ukrainians and Belarusians. It is the fourth time Poland has been divided among its neighbours since 1772.

events.title: The Winter War ends: Finland loses Karelia
events.text: After the 105-day Winter War that began with the Soviet invasion of 30 November 1939, Finland signs the Moscow Peace Treaty on 12 March 1940. It cedes the Karelian Isthmus, Vyborg and land around Lake Ladoga, roughly a tenth of its territory, and about 400,000 Karelians are evacuated. Despite the Red Army's size, Finland keeps its independence.

events.title: The USSR takes Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina
events.text: After an ultimatum of 26 June 1940, Romania gives Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union on 28 June, territories the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact had placed in the Soviet sphere. Bessarabia, today's Moldova, becomes the Moldavian SSR in August, while Northern Bukovina is joined to Soviet Ukraine.

events.title: The Soviet Union annexes the Baltic states
events.text: After the Soviet occupation of June 1940 and elections held under Soviet control, Lithuania (3 August), Latvia (5 August) and Estonia (6 August) are annexed by the USSR as Soviet republics. The United States and many other governments refused to recognise the annexations. Tens of thousands were deported in the following year, and the three countries regained independence in 1991.

events.title: Second Vienna Award: Hungary gets Northern Transylvania
events.text: Germany and Italy arbitrate the Second Vienna Award on 30 August 1940, forcing Romania to give Hungary about 43,000 square kilometres of Northern Transylvania, where Romanians and Hungarians both lived. It satisfied neither side, and the region returned to Romania after the war.

events.title: Treaty of Craiova: Bulgaria regains Southern Dobruja
events.text: By the Treaty of Craiova of 7 September 1940, Romania returns Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria, which had lost it in 1913. The treaty was signed with German and Italian encouragement and included an exchange of populations. Bulgaria kept the region after the war.

events.title: Yugoslavia and Greece are carved up
events.text: Germany, Italy, Hungary and Bulgaria invade Yugoslavia and Greece on 6 April 1941; Yugoslavia surrenders on 17 April and Greece falls by the end of the month. Yugoslavia is divided: Croatia becomes a German- and Italian-backed puppet state, Serbia is placed under German military rule, and neighbouring Axis powers annex border regions. Greece is split into German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation zones. Both countries soon see strong resistance movements.

events.title: Ethiopia is liberated
events.text: British, Commonwealth and Ethiopian forces drive the Italians out of East Africa in the campaign of 1940-41, and Emperor Haile Selassie re-enters Addis Ababa on 5 May 1941, five years to the day after Italian troops first entered it. Ethiopia is restored as an independent state, while Eritrea and Italian Somaliland come under British military administration.

events.title: Germany occupies the western Soviet Union
events.text: Germany invades the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941 in Operation Barbarossa and advances hundreds of kilometres in weeks. In the occupied lands the Nazis set up civil administrations: Reichskommissariat Ostland covers the Baltic states and Belarus, and Reichskommissariat Ukraine follows in September. The occupation brought mass killings of Jews and civilians and famine, and the Soviet Union lost more than twenty million people in the war.

events.title: Iceland becomes a republic
events.text: Iceland, in a personal union with Denmark since 1918 and occupied by the Allies in 1940, votes overwhelmingly to cut its last ties to the Danish crown and proclaims a republic on 17 June 1944, the birthday of independence hero Jon Sigurdsson.

events.title: Victory in Europe: the Axis conquests are undone
events.text: Germany surrenders unconditionally on 7-8 May 1945, ending the war in Europe. The countries the Axis had conquered or carved up are restored: Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Albania, Greece and Austria return, and the Soviet-occupied lands return to Soviet control. Austria is separated from Germany again and put under four-power occupation. Transcarpathia, taken by Hungary in 1939 and by the Red Army in 1944, is ceded by Czechoslovakia to Soviet Ukraine in June 1945.

events.title: Potsdam: Germany is divided and Poland moves west
events.text: At the Potsdam Conference (17 July to 2 August 1945), Truman, Stalin and Attlee decide how to run defeated Germany. It is divided into four occupation zones, and Berlin is divided too. The Soviet Union keeps the northern half of East Prussia around Konigsberg, later Kaliningrad, and Poland's western border moves to the Oder-Neisse line, while Poland loses its eastern lands to the USSR. About twelve million Germans were expelled or fled from these and other eastern territories, one of the largest forced migrations in history.

events.title: Japan surrenders and its empire is dismantled
events.text: Japan formally surrenders on 2 September 1945 aboard the USS Missouri, ending the Second World War. Its empire is broken up: Taiwan and Manchuria return to China, South Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands are taken by the Soviet Union (Japan still disputes the southern Kurils), and Korea, freed from 35 years of Japanese rule, is divided into Soviet and American occupation zones at the 38th parallel. Japan's Pacific mandates later become a US trust territory, and Japan is occupied by US forces until 1952.

events.title: Syria, Lebanon and Transjordan become independent
events.text: The last French troops leave Syria on 17 April 1946, and Lebanon, which proclaimed independence in 1943, sees the last French soldiers withdraw by the end of the year. On 25 May 1946 Britain recognises Transjordan as an independent kingdom under Abdullah I.

events.title: The Philippines become independent
events.text: The United States grants independence to the Philippines on 4 July 1946, after nearly half a century of American rule that began in 1898 and the Japanese occupation of the Second World War. The date was chosen to match US Independence Day; the Philippines later moved its own Independence Day to 12 June.

events.title: The Paris Peace Treaties
events.text: The Paris Peace Treaties, signed on 10 February 1947, settle the post-war borders of Italy, Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Finland. Italy gives Istria and most of Venezia Giulia to Yugoslavia, gives up its colonies, and hands the Dodecanese to Greece. Romania keeps Transylvania, Hungary returns to its 1938 borders, Bulgaria keeps Southern Dobruja, and Finland confirms its losses to the USSR.

events.title: The partition of India
events.text: Britain ends its rule over the Indian subcontinent on 14-15 August 1947 by creating two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, with a border drawn in a few weeks by Cyril Radcliffe. Pakistan has two parts, West Pakistan and East Bengal, about 1,600 kilometres apart. Partition triggered one of the largest migrations in history, with an estimated 10 to 20 million people crossing the new border, and estimates of deaths range from several hundred thousand to two million.

events.title: Burma and Ceylon become independent
events.text: Burma becomes independent on 4 January 1948 and leaves the British Commonwealth, while Ceylon, today's Sri Lanka, becomes a self-governing dominion on 4 February 1948 and stays in it. Burma's new government faced rebellions from the start, and the country is today called Myanmar.

events.title: The State of Israel is proclaimed
events.text: On 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate for Palestine expires, David Ben-Gurion proclaims the State of Israel. Neighbouring Arab states attack the next day, and the war ends with armistice agreements in 1949. Jordan takes control of the West Bank and East Jerusalem and Egypt of the Gaza Strip, while about 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba.

events.title: Korea splits into two states
events.text: The Republic of Korea is proclaimed in the south on 15 August 1948 and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in the north on 9 September, each claiming to govern the whole peninsula. The division, meant to be temporary in 1945, hardens as the Cold War begins. The Korean War of 1950-53 ends in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, and the border remains one of the most heavily fortified in the world.

events.title: Ireland becomes a republic
events.text: The Republic of Ireland Act comes into force on 18 April 1949, ending the Irish Free State's last links to the British Crown and leading Ireland to leave the Commonwealth. Northern Ireland stays part of the United Kingdom.

events.title: The People's Republic of China
events.text: After winning the Chinese Civil War, Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China in Beijing on 1 October 1949. The defeated Nationalist government of the Republic of China retreats to Taiwan in December and continues to govern it and a few small islands. Both governments claimed to be the legitimate government of China, and the status of Taiwan remains unresolved; the PRC took China's seat at the United Nations in 1971.

events.title: Germany splits into East and West
events.text: The Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) is founded on 23 May 1949, and the Soviet-backed German Democratic Republic (East Germany) follows on 7 October 1949. Berlin, deep inside East German territory, stays divided between the two sides. About 3.5 million people left East Germany for the West over the next decades, and the Berlin Wall of 1961 was built to stop them.

events.title: Indonesia becomes independent
events.text: After four years of war and negotiation, the Netherlands formally transfers sovereignty over the Dutch East Indies to Indonesia on 27 December 1949; Sukarno had proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch keep Western New Guinea, which Indonesia also claims, until 1962.

events.title: Tibet comes under Chinese control
events.text: The People's Liberation Army enters the Tibetan region of Chamdo in October 1950. On 23 May 1951, Tibetan representatives sign the Seventeen Point Agreement in Beijing, which recognises Chinese sovereignty over Tibet; the Tibetan government later said it was signed under pressure. The Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959 after a failed uprising.

events.title: Libya becomes independent
events.text: Libya becomes independent as a united kingdom under King Idris on 24 December 1951, the first country to gain independence through a decision of the United Nations. It had been under British and French military administration since Italy's defeat in 1943, and Italy renounced it in the 1947 peace treaty. Oil discovered in 1959 would later transform its economy.

events.title: The occupation of Japan ends
events.text: The Treaty of San Francisco takes effect on 28 April 1952, ending the Allied occupation led by the United States and restoring Japanese sovereignty. Japan renounces its former colonies, and the US keeps control of Okinawa until 1972.

events.title: Eritrea is federated with Ethiopia
events.text: Under a UN resolution, Eritrea, a former Italian colony then run by Britain, is federated with Ethiopia on 11 September 1952 with its own parliament. Ethiopia dissolved the federation in 1962 and annexed Eritrea outright, which led to a 30-year war of independence. Italian Somaliland, meanwhile, was a UN trust territory under Italian administration from 1950 to 1960.

events.title: Geneva Accords: Vietnam is divided
events.text: After France's defeat at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954, the Geneva Accords of 21 July end the First Indochina War. Vietnam is temporarily divided at the 17th parallel into a communist north under Ho Chi Minh and a non-communist south. Elections for reunification were planned for 1956 but never held. Laos and Cambodia, which had gained independence in 1953, are recognised as separate countries.

events.title: Austria regains full independence
events.text: On 15 May 1955 the four occupying powers sign the Austrian State Treaty, ending ten years of occupation. Austria promises permanent neutrality, which the parliament declares in October after the last foreign troops leave.

events.title: Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia become independent
events.text: Sudan becomes independent on 1 January 1956, ending joint British-Egyptian rule, and France recognises Morocco's independence on 2 March and Tunisia's on 20 March. Both were French protectorates rather than colonies, which made independence faster than in Algeria. Spain gave up its northern protectorate in Morocco in April 1956.

events.title: Ghana: the first independent state in sub-Saharan Africa
events.text: The Gold Coast becomes independent as Ghana on 6 March 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence from European rule. Its example inspired independence movements across the continent, and Nkrumah became a leading voice of pan-Africanism.

events.title: Malaya becomes independent
events.text: The Federation of Malaya becomes independent from Britain on 31 August 1957, after a long communist insurgency known as the Malayan Emergency. Singapore and the Borneo territories of Sarawak and North Borneo remain under British control for now.

events.title: Egypt and Syria form the United Arab Republic
events.text: Egypt and Syria merge into the United Arab Republic on 1 February 1958 under Gamal Abdel Nasser, a step toward Arab unity even though the two countries did not share a border. Syria withdrew after a coup on 28 September 1961, ending the union, and Egypt kept the name until 1971.

events.title: The monarchy falls in Iraq
events.text: On 14 July 1958 army officers led by Abd al-Karim Qasim overthrow the Hashemite monarchy of Iraq, killing King Faisal II, and proclaim a republic. The coup took Iraq out of the Baghdad Pact with Britain, Turkey and Iran.

events.title: Guinea says no to France
events.text: Guinea votes 'no' in de Gaulle's 1958 referendum on joining a new French Community and becomes independent on 2 October 1958 under Sekou Toure. France withdrew its administrators and equipment in anger, and Guinea became the first French West African colony to leave. Other French territories followed in 1960.

events.title: 1960: the Year of Africa
events.text: Seventeen African countries become independent in 1960. Cameroon (1 January), Togo (27 April), Madagascar (26 June), the Belgian Congo (30 June), Somalia (1 July), most of France's colonies in West and Central Africa (all in August), Nigeria (1 October) and Mauritania (28 November). British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan had spoken of a 'wind of change' blowing through the continent in February. Cyprus also became independent from Britain on 16 August 1960.

events.title: 1961: Sierra Leone, Kuwait, Cameroon and Tanganyika
events.text: Sierra Leone becomes independent on 27 April 1961 and Kuwait on 19 June. Southern Cameroons votes on 1 October to join Cameroon, while Northern Cameroons has chosen to join Nigeria. Syria leaves the United Arab Republic after a coup on 28 September, and Tanganyika becomes independent on 9 December. Tanganyika would merge with Zanzibar in 1964 to form Tanzania.

events.title: Algeria wins independence
events.text: Algeria becomes independent on 5 July 1962, after an eight-year war (1954-62), the Evian Accords of March and a referendum on 1 July. Algeria had been legally part of France rather than a colony and had about a million European settlers, most of whom left within months. Rwanda and Burundi, formerly Belgian-administered territories, also became independent on 1 July 1962.

events.title: Uganda, Jamaica, Trinidad and Western Samoa
events.text: Uganda becomes independent on 9 October 1962. Earlier that year Western Samoa (1 January), Jamaica (6 August) and Trinidad and Tobago (31 August) had also left colonial rule, the first independent states in their regions to emerge from British and New Zealand administration in this wave.

events.title: Western New Guinea passes to Indonesia
events.text: After pressure from Indonesia and the United States, the Netherlands agrees to hand Western New Guinea to a UN administration in 1962, which transfers it to Indonesia on 1 May 1963. A 1969 vote, the 'Act of Free Choice', was held with about a thousand selected representatives and is widely criticised, and the region remains the scene of a separatist conflict.

events.title: Malaysia is formed
events.text: Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo (Sabah) join together as Malaysia on 16 September 1963; Brunei decided to stay out. Indonesia opposed the federation and waged an undeclared 'Confrontation' against it until 1966.

events.title: Kenya becomes independent
events.text: Kenya becomes independent on 12 December 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, after the Mau Mau uprising of 1952-60 and a harsh British counter-insurgency campaign. Zanzibar had become independent two days earlier.

events.title: Tanzania, Malawi, Malta and Zambia
events.text: In 1964 Tanganyika and Zanzibar merge as Tanzania (26 April), Nyasaland becomes Malawi (6 July), Malta becomes independent (21 September) and Northern Rhodesia becomes Zambia (24 October).

events.title: Singapore becomes independent
events.text: Singapore is separated from Malaysia on 9 August 1965 and becomes an independent republic after tensions between the Malay-dominated federal government and Singapore's mainly ethnic Chinese leaders. Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew wept as he announced it on television. With few natural resources, Singapore became one of the world's wealthiest countries.

events.title: Independence in southern Africa, the Caribbean and Arabia
events.text: The Gambia (1965), Guyana and Botswana and Lesotho (1966), Barbados (1966), South Yemen (30 November 1967), Nauru (31 January 1968), Mauritius (12 March 1968), Swaziland (6 September 1968) and Equatorial Guinea (12 October 1968) all become independent in these years, as Britain and Spain wind down their remaining colonies in these regions.

events.title: Oman
events.text: Sultan Qaboos bin Said overthrows his father in a palace coup on 23 July 1970 and renames Muscat and Oman as the Sultanate of Oman. He begins modernising a country that had only a handful of schools and hospitals, and rules until 2020.

events.title: Tonga and Fiji become independent
events.text: Tonga, a British protected state, regains full independence on 4 June 1970, and Fiji becomes independent on 10 October 1970 after nearly a century as a British colony.

events.title: Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates
events.text: Britain withdraws from its commitments east of Suez, and in 1971 Bahrain (15 August), Qatar (3 September) and the United Arab Emirates (2 December) become independent. The UAE begins as a federation of six emirates, with Ras al-Khaimah joining in early 1972.

events.title: Bangladesh is born
events.text: After Pakistan's army cracked down on Bengali nationalists in March 1971, millions fled to India and a war of independence began. India intervened in December, and Pakistani forces in the east surrendered on 16 December 1971, creating Bangladesh from what had been East Pakistan. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to three million.

events.title: Ceylon becomes Sri Lanka
events.text: Ceylon adopts a new constitution on 22 May 1972, becomes a republic and takes the name Sri Lanka. A civil war between the government and Tamil separatists began in 1983 and lasted until 2009.

events.title: Greece abolishes its monarchy
events.text: After the fall of the military junta of 1967-74, Greeks vote on 8 December 1974 in a referendum against restoring the monarchy, and the Third Hellenic Republic is established. The same year, Turkey invaded Cyprus, dividing the island.

events.title: The end of the Portuguese empire in Africa
events.text: Portugal's Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 overthrows its dictatorship and ends its colonial wars, which had lasted over a decade. Guinea-Bissau (recognised in 1974), Mozambique (25 June 1975), Cape Verde (5 July), Sao Tome and Principe (12 July) and Angola (11 November) become independent. Angola falls straight into a civil war that lasts until 2002.

events.title: Dahomey becomes Benin
events.text: Dahomey, independent since 1960, is renamed Benin on 30 November 1975 by its Marxist-Leninist government, after the Bight of Benin rather than the old Kingdom of Benin, which was in today's Nigeria.

events.title: Indonesia invades East Timor
events.text: Portuguese Timor declares independence on 28 November 1975, and Indonesia invades on 7 December and annexes it as a province in 1976. The United Nations never recognised the annexation. Between 100,000 and 200,000 people are estimated to have died in the occupation from violence, hunger and disease.

events.title: Western Sahara is divided between Morocco and Mauritania
events.text: Spain withdraws from Spanish Sahara in early 1976 after the Madrid Accords of November 1975 and Morocco's Green March. Morocco and Mauritania divide the territory on 14 April 1976, but the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, declares the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic and fights both. The status of Western Sahara remains disputed, and the UN lists it as a non-self-governing territory.

events.title: Vietnam is reunified
events.text: After the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 ended the Vietnam War, North and South Vietnam are officially reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam on 2 July 1976. The war had killed well over a million Vietnamese, and US forces had withdrawn in 1973.

events.title: Comoros, Seychelles and Djibouti
events.text: The Comoros declare independence on 6 July 1975, the Seychelles become independent on 29 June 1976, and Djibouti, the former French Somaliland, becomes independent on 27 June 1977.

events.title: Mauritania gives up its part of Western Sahara
events.text: Mauritania, worn down by the war with the Polisario Front, signs a peace agreement in Algiers on 5 August 1979 and renounces its claim. Morocco immediately occupies the area it had held, and now controls most of Western Sahara, behind a long defensive wall.

events.title: Zimbabwe becomes independent
events.text: Southern Rhodesia, whose white minority government had declared independence from Britain in 1965, becomes Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980 after a guerrilla war and the Lancaster House Agreement of 1979. Robert Mugabe, its first prime minister, ruled until he was forced out in 2017.

events.title: The last island colonies become independent
events.text: Between 1973 and 1984 most of the remaining Caribbean and Pacific colonies become independent: the Bahamas (1973), Grenada (1974), Papua New Guinea (1975), Suriname (1975), the Solomon Islands and Tuvalu (1978), Dominica (1978), Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent (1979), Kiribati (1979), Vanuatu (1980), Belize and Antigua and Barbuda (1981), Saint Kitts and Nevis (1983) and Brunei (1 January 1984).

events.title: Upper Volta becomes Burkina Faso
events.text: President Thomas Sankara renames Upper Volta as Burkina Faso, meaning the land of upright people, on 4 August 1984, the first anniversary of his coming to power. Sankara was killed in a coup in 1987.

events.title: Burma becomes Myanmar
events.text: Burma's military government changes the English name of the country to Myanmar on 18 June 1989, after the crushing of the 1988 democracy uprising. Some governments and opposition groups kept using Burma for years afterward.

events.title: Namibia becomes independent
events.text: Namibia becomes independent on 21 March 1990, the last colony in Africa to do so, after a long armed struggle led by SWAPO and a UN-supervised transition. South Africa had ruled the territory since 1915 and refused to leave after the League of Nations mandate ended; the port of Walvis Bay was handed over in 1994.

events.title: Yemen is unified
events.text: North Yemen and South Yemen unite as the Republic of Yemen on 22 May 1990. The union followed the end of the Cold War, but tensions led to a brief civil war in 1994, and conflict has returned since 2014.

events.title: German reunification
events.text: East Germany joins the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990, less than a year after the Berlin Wall opened on 9 November 1989. The Two Plus Four Treaty, signed in September 1990 by the two German states and the four wartime allies, confirmed the Oder-Neisse border with Poland and the full sovereignty of united Germany.

events.title: Slovenia and Croatia leave Yugoslavia
events.text: Slovenia and Croatia declare independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991. Slovenia's Ten-Day War ends quickly with the withdrawal of the Yugoslav army, while the war in Croatia lasts until 1995. The breakup of Yugoslavia, driven by nationalism after Tito's death in 1980 and the fall of communism, became Europe's deadliest conflict since 1945.

events.title: The Baltic states regain their independence
events.text: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared the restoration of independence in 1990-91, and the Soviet State Council formally recognises them on 6 September 1991, after the failed hardliners' coup in Moscow in August. The Baltic Way, a human chain of about two million people across the three republics on 23 August 1989, marked the 50th anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact.

events.title: The Soviet Union dissolves
events.text: On 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union ceases to exist, a day after Mikhail Gorbachev resigns as president. Fifteen independent states emerge: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and the three Baltic states already recognised. The leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus had declared the union dissolved at Belovezha on 8 December. Ukraine inherits Crimea, which had been transferred from the Russian to the Ukrainian republic in 1954.

events.title: North Macedonia and Bosnia leave; Serbia and Montenegro remain
events.text: North Macedonia (referendum of 8 September 1991) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (independence declared 3 March 1992) leave Yugoslavia, and Serbia and Montenegro form the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April 1992. The Bosnian War of 1992-95, which included the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica massacre of July 1995, ends with the Dayton Agreement signed in December 1995. Greece disputed North Macedonia's name until 2019.

events.title: Czechoslovakia splits peacefully
events.text: Czechoslovakia splits into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, in what is known as the Velvet Divorce, three years after the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule. The split was decided by politicians rather than by a referendum, and it was almost entirely free of violence.

events.title: Eritrea becomes independent
events.text: Eritrea becomes independent from Ethiopia on 24 May 1993 after a 30-year war and a UN-observed referendum in April in which almost everyone voted for independence. A border war with Ethiopia followed in 1998-2000.

events.title: Hong Kong returns to China
events.text: Britain returns Hong Kong to China on 1 July 1997, when the 99-year lease on the New Territories ends. China promises to govern it as a Special Administrative Region under the principle of 'one country, two systems' for 50 years, keeping its own legal and economic systems.

events.title: Macau returns to China
events.text: Portugal hands Macau back to China on 20 December 1999, ending more than four centuries of Portuguese presence that began in the 16th century. Like Hong Kong, Macau becomes a Special Administrative Region.

events.title: East Timor becomes independent
events.text: East Timor votes for independence in a UN-run referendum on 30 August 1999, followed by violence by pro-Indonesian militias. After a period of UN administration, it becomes fully independent as Timor-Leste on 20 May 2002.

events.title: Montenegro becomes independent
events.text: Montenegro declares independence on 3 June 2006 after a referendum on 21 May in which 55.5 percent voted yes, just above the 55 percent threshold set by the European Union. This ended the last remnant of Yugoslavia, the loose union of Serbia and Montenegro created in 2003.

events.title: Kosovo declares independence
events.text: Kosovo, a province of Serbia with a large ethnic Albanian majority and under UN administration since the 1999 NATO intervention, declares independence on 17 February 2008. More than 100 UN member states recognise it, but Serbia, Russia, China and several EU members do not, and it is not a UN member. The International Court of Justice advised in 2010 that the declaration did not violate international law.

events.title: South Sudan becomes independent
events.text: South Sudan becomes the world's newest country on 9 July 2011, after almost 99 percent of voters chose independence in a January referendum, following a 2005 peace agreement that ended Sudan's second civil war. A new civil war began in South Sudan in December 2013.

events.title: Russia annexes Crimea
events.text: Russia annexes Crimea on 18 March 2014 after its forces took control of the peninsula and a referendum was held under their control. Ukraine and most countries, including a UN General Assembly resolution (68/262), regard Crimea as Ukrainian territory under occupation, while Russia treats it as part of the Russian Federation. This map shows who controls the territory in practice, not which governments recognise it.
